historical_timeline.summary: Born at Springwood in Hyde Park, New York.
Father died during his first term at Harvard.
Paralytic illness diagnosed as infantile paralysis; paraplegic thereafter.
Examined at Bethesda Naval Hospital: hypertension, enlarged heart, and congestive heart failure.
Died of a cerebral hemorrhage at Warm Springs, Georgia.

claims.statement: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, at Springwood, the family's estate in Hyde Park, New York.
Roosevelt died of a cerebral hemorrhage at Warm Springs, Georgia, on April 12, 1945, aged 63.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: In the summer of 1921 Roosevelt developed a paralytic illness at Campobello; on August 25, 1921, Dr. Robert Lovett diagnosed infantile paralysis (polio), and Roosevelt remained paraplegic, using leg braces from early 1922.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The contemporaneous diagnosis was polio; a later retrospective analysis proposes another cause.

claims.statement: A 2003 Bayesian analysis of the recorded symptoms concluded that Guillain-Barré syndrome was more probable than paralytic polio as the cause of Roosevelt's 1921 illness; the conclusion is disputed and cannot be confirmed because no cerebrospinal fluid was examined.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Keep the cause contested; the modern problem list records sequelae of the documented 1921 diagnosis.

source_links.locator: Abstract: six of eight posterior probabilities favored Guillain-Barré syndrome

claims.statement: In May 1941 Roosevelt had severe iron deficiency anemia, with hemoglobin reported at 4.5 g/100 mL.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Reported in a secondary medical account; the primary record was not reviewed.

claims.statement: At an examination at Bethesda Naval Hospital on March 27, 1944, Roosevelt's blood pressure was 186/108; he was breathless and cyanotic with rales, and X-rays and an electrocardiogram showed an enlarged heart, congestive heart failure, and a mitral murmur. His blood pressure had not been checked since February 27, 1941.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the synthetic hypertensive heart failure episode.

source_links.locator: Bruenn's 1970 clinical account, cited by both secondary sources; full text not reviewed

claims.statement: After the March 1944 examination Roosevelt was treated with digitalis, a low-sodium and weight-reduction diet, and rest; his working hours were reduced, his cigarettes were limited to ten a day, and his evening cocktails were reduced.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents tobacco use and the era's limited treatment options; no antihypertensive drugs were available.

claims.statement: Roosevelt's blood pressure remained severely elevated, reported up to 260/150 in February 1945 and ranging from 170/88 to 240/130 at Warm Springs before his death.
Roosevelt's father, James Roosevelt, died in 1900 during Franklin's first term at Harvard; his mother, Sara Delano Roosevelt, died at Springwood in September 1941.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cited source does not give causes of death.

encounters.display: Same-day sick visit for vomiting and diarrhea

documentation.chief_complaint: Vomiting and watery diarrhea for two days, with lightheadedness on transfers

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roosevelt is a 62-year-old man with hypertensive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction 30 percent at the April echocardiogram), now compensated on sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, and empagliflozin, who uses a manual wheelchair after a paralytic illness at age 39. He asked for a same-day visit. Two days ago, the evening after a large working dinner, he developed nausea and vomited three times overnight, followed by watery diarrhea six to eight times a day. Several other guests at the dinner have had a similar illness. The vomiting stopped yesterday morning and he is keeping down sips of water and broth, but he has eaten little. There has been no blood or black stool. His highest home temperature was 37.8 °C. His urine is darker and less frequent. This morning he felt lightheaded when moving from his bed to his wheelchair and needed help to complete the transfer; he did not fall. He took all of his usual morning medicines today. He has had no chest pain, and he is not more breathless than usual and still sleeps on one pillow. He has taken nothing for the diarrhea.

Nausea, vomiting on the first night only, watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain; no blood, black stool, or severe constant pain
Darker, less frequent urine; no dysuria
No chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, or leg swelling
No cough; breathing at his usual baseline
Lightheaded on transfers this morning; no syncope, confusion, or headache
No skin breakdown noticed over the sacrum or buttocks

exam.finding: Tired but alert and conversant; seated in his wheelchair, transferred to the examination table with a transfer board and one assistant

exam.system: Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat
exam.finding: Dry mucous membranes
Jugular venous pressure not visible above the clavicle at 45 degrees
Regular rhythm, rate 86; no S3; capillary refill about 3 seconds
Clear to auscultation; no crackles
Soft, mildly and diffusely tender without guarding or rebound; hyperactive bowel sounds; no distension
No leg or sacral edema
Sacral, ischial, and perineal skin intact; no pressure injury or moisture-associated skin damage
Seated 102/64 mmHg, pulse 86; standing orthostatic readings not possible because of his paraplegia

assessment_plan.display: Acute viral gastroenteritis with mild volume depletion
assessment_plan.assessment: A likely norovirus-type illness given the short incubation, vomiting followed by watery diarrhea, and other people ill after the same meal. There is no blood in the stool, high fever, or severe pain, so stool testing and antibiotics are not indicated. Dry mucous membranes, low-normal blood pressure, and a 2.4 kg weight loss since June point to mild volume depletion that oral fluids can correct
plan: Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent sips, about 200 mL after each loose stool, then a normal diet as tolerated
Loperamide 4 mg once, then 2 mg after each loose stool, up to 8 mg a day, only while the stool has no blood and the temperature stays below 38.5 °C
Hand washing with soap and water, because alcohol gel is less effective against norovirus; bathroom surfaces cleaned with a bleach-based cleaner
Same-day basic metabolic panel

assessment_plan.display: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
assessment_plan.assessment: Euvolemic to dry, with no signs of congestion. Potassium 4.9 mmol/L is at the upper end of normal and creatinine 1.42 mg/dL is up from 1.24 in June, a rise below the threshold for acute kidney injury, consistent with volume depletion while on renin-angiotensin, mineralocorticoid, and SGLT2 blockade
plan: Sick-day rule: hold empagliflozin, spironolactone, and sacubitril/valsartan from tonight until he has been eating and drinking normally for 24 hours, then restart all three at the usual doses

Continue carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily with food, because stopping a beta-blocker abruptly can destabilize heart failure. Skip a single dose only if the seated systolic pressure on his home monitor is below 90 mmHg or he is lightheaded at rest
Continue atorvastatin
After restarting, call for breathlessness, needing extra pillows, or new leg swelling

If the diarrhea lasts beyond 48 hours or he cannot restart the held medicines by then, return for a repeat basic metabolic panel; otherwise potassium and creatinine are rechecked at the September review

assessment_plan.assessment: Blood pressure 102/64 mmHg seated, lower than his usual 120s systolic because of volume depletion
plan: No change in long-term treatment; the temporary holds above cover today's lower pressure

assessment_plan.display: Paraplegia after a paralytic illness at age 39; uses a manual wheelchair
assessment_plan.assessment: Lightheadedness and frequent toileting raise his risk of a transfer fall and of moisture-related skin damage over pressure areas
plan: Sit at the edge of the bed for a minute before each transfer, use the transfer board, and have someone present for transfers until he is drinking normally
Barrier cream to the perineal and sacral skin after each stool, and a daily skin check with a mirror or a helper
Keep up pressure relief in the wheelchair

documentation.follow_up: Nurse telephone check tomorrow. Call or return the same day for blood in the stool, a temperature of 38.5 °C or higher, being unable to keep fluids down, passing no urine for eight hours, lightheadedness at rest, a fall, or breathlessness or leg swelling after restarting his medicines

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roosevelt comes for his periodic preventive visit four weeks after his six-month heart failure review, at which the ejection fraction had improved to 45 percent. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit. The viral gastroenteritis in July settled within four days; he restarted all of his heart failure medicines on the third day without lightheadedness. He has had no emergency visits or hospital stays, no falls or transfer slips, and no skin breakdown. He has not smoked since April and finished the nicotine patch course in June; he reports occasional cravings during long meetings, which pass. He takes his medicines from a weekly organizer and has added no over-the-counter medicines or supplements. He has no new concerns.

health_risk_assessment.finding: Good, and much better than in the spring
Lives with his spouse; strong support from family and staff; work is demanding but he feels in control of it
Former smoker with more than 30 pack-years; quit six months ago
One cocktail on some evenings; never more than two; AUDIT-C score 2
Seated upper-body exercise with resistance bands three times a week, plus daily wheelchair propulsion
Follows the low-sodium plan; eats out at working dinners several times a week
About seven hours on one pillow; no snoring concerns raised
Independent in eating, grooming, upper-body dressing, and transfers with a transfer board; uses a roll-in shower with a shower chair; help with lower-body dressing
Manages his own medicines, finances, and correspondence; travels with an assistant
Ramped entrances, grab bars by the toilet and shower, smoke detectors working; wheelchair cushion replaced this year
Reading glasses; last eye examination more than two years ago; no hearing concerns
Wears a seat belt when traveling by car; no firearms in the home

ros.finding: Weight stable at 82 kg on the wheelchair scale; no fatigue, fever, or night sweats
No change in vision with reading glasses
No hearing loss, hoarseness, or mouth sores
No chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, or leg swelling
The morning cough he had while smoking has gone; no breathlessness when propelling his wheelchair on level ground
Bowel habit back to his usual since July; no blood in the stool or black stool
No urinary symptoms; no nighttime urination beyond once
Lower-limb weakness unchanged from his baseline; no shoulder, elbow, or wrist pain with propelling or transfers
No redness or breakdown over the sacrum, ischial areas, or heels
No new weakness or numbness in the arms, headache, or dizziness
Mood good; sleeping well; PHQ-2 score 0
No polyuria, polydipsia, or heat or cold intolerance
No easy bruising or bleeding

exam.finding: Alert, well-appearing, and good-humored; seated in his wheelchair; weight 82.0 kg on the wheelchair scale
Pupils equal and reactive; near vision 20/25 with reading glasses
Canals and tympanic membranes normal; oropharynx clear; dentition in good repair
No thyroid enlargement or nodes; no carotid bruits; jugular venous pressure not raised
Regular rhythm, rate 62; no S3; radial pulses normal; no edema
Clear to auscultation bilaterally; no wheeze
Soft and non-tender; no masses, organ enlargement, or aortic bruit
Shoulders: full range of motion, strength 5/5, and no impingement signs. Lower limbs: weakness and muscle wasting unchanged from his baseline
Sacral, ischial, and heel skin intact with no pressure injury; wheelchair cushion in good condition and correctly inflated
Alert and oriented; upper-limb strength, sensation, and reflexes normal
Euthymic and engaged; judgment and insight intact

assessment_plan.assessment: Health risk assessment reviewed and a written prevention plan given. Depression and alcohol screens are negative. Because he has smoked more than 20 pack-years and quit less than 15 years ago, he qualifies for annual lung cancer screening
plan: Next preventive visit in one year

assessment_plan.display: Heart failure with improved ejection fraction
assessment_plan.assessment: Ejection fraction 45 percent in September, up from 30 percent; KCCQ-12 78 and no congestion today. Guideline-directed therapy continues even though the ejection fraction has improved
plan: Continue sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, empagliflozin, and atorvastatin without change
Heart failure review with a basic metabolic panel in about three months, on the CMID schedule

assessment_plan.assessment: Blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, below the 130/80 target
plan: No change

assessment_plan.display: Nicotine dependence, cigarettes, in early remission
assessment_plan.assessment: Abstinent for six months with brief cravings that pass
plan: Relapse-prevention counseling given; restart a nicotine patch with a short-acting nicotine product at once if he smokes again
Low-dose CT lung cancer screening after shared decision-making, below

assessment_plan.assessment: HbA1c 5.9 percent in March, with glucose values since then between 92 and 98 mg/dL
plan: Repeat HbA1c with the heart failure laboratory tests in about three months
Continue the low-sodium diet and seated exercise program

assessment_plan.display: Paraplegia after a paralytic illness at age 39; uses a manual wheelchair
assessment_plan.assessment: Skin intact and shoulders pain-free. Upper-limb overuse and pressure injury are the main long-term risks for a manual wheelchair user
plan: Pressure relief every 15 to 30 minutes while seated and a daily skin check
Use the transfer board and keep transfers level where possible to protect the shoulders
Seating and wheelchair review by occupational therapy in one year, or sooner for shoulder pain

prevention_plan.detail: Dose 1 of 2 given today; dose 2 due in two to six months
Discussed; he plans to get this season's vaccine at his pharmacy
Discussed because heart failure increases his risk of severe RSV illness; he will decide at the pharmacy visit
PCV20 given in April; no further doses needed
Tdap five and a half years ago; next booster due in about four and a half years
More than 30 pack-years and quit six months ago. After shared decision-making about benefits, false positives, and radiation, he chose annual low-dose CT; first scan ordered

No prior screening on record. Options discussed; because bowel preparation and the toileting it requires are hard for him, he chose a yearly fecal immunochemical test, and a kit was given today. A positive test needs colonoscopy
Shared decision-making about the small benefit and the risks of overdiagnosis; he chose not to have PSA testing now and will revisit it next year
One-time screening recommended for all adults in these age ranges; no prior result on record; added to the next blood draw
Not yet; a one-time ultrasound is recommended between 65 and 75 for men who have ever smoked

prevention_plan.service: Blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes screening
prevention_plan.detail: Treated hypertension and hyperlipidemia on statin therapy, LDL cholesterol 68 mg/dL in September; prediabetes followed with yearly HbA1c
AUDIT-C score 2; below the threshold for men; advice to keep to two drinks or fewer on any day
More than two years since his last examination; he will book with his optometrist

documentation.advance_care_planning: Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with his consent, prompted by his heart failure diagnosis. He has named a health care agent and agreed to complete a written health care directive naming that person; a blank form was given today. He wants full treatment, including hospital and intensive care, for any condition from which he could return to his work and present independence. He would not want prolonged life support if he could not communicate or recover. He will discuss these wishes with his agent and bring the completed form to his next visit.
documentation.follow_up: Low-dose CT scan, stool test kit, and hepatitis C and HIV screening ordered. Zoster vaccine dose 2 in two to six months. Heart failure review with laboratory tests in about three months. Next preventive visit in one year
